The tool was evaluated on 452 Circom circuits on a Xeon 2.20GHz CPU with 31GB RAM against Circomspect, ZKAP, Picus and ConsCS, and the code is on GitHub. Section 8 discusses limitations and future work.

rq3.speedup_and_baseline: zkFuzz++ found 85 of 88 bugs with 0 FP, versus Circomspect 63 TP/74 FP, ZKAP 43/41, Picus 22-23/0 and ConsCS 14/0 (30-300% more bugs). It found 90% of bugs within 100 s, more than 30x faster than core zkFuzz.

rq4.proof_system_used: Circom/R1CS circuits (snarkjs); Noir ACIR/Brillig
rq4.reason_for_choice: Circom is the most popular ZK DSL; Noir is an emerging DSL

cq.note: TCCT covers both under-constrained (soundness) bugs, including computation aborts, and over-constrained (completeness) bugs. It found 59 zero-days, 39 confirmed and 14 fixed. Static analysis is used only as target selectors in zkFuzz++.

rq5.limitations: Execution time grows with the size of the target program. The Noir prototype is preliminary and has no guiding or target selectors.
rq5.open_problems: Add target selectors for Noir and extend the tool to other DSLs through common formats like R1CS. Combine it with formal verification, static analysis and ML-based bug detection.

eligibility.note: The paper is about verifying quantitative hyperproperties in general; a toy interactive ZK puzzle (ZK Hats) is only one of five case studies, so ZKPs are neither its main subject nor a core mechanism.

qa.evidence: The contributions are listed explicitly and verification times are measured on an Intel i7-4770 with 32 GB RAM. Lemmas are stated, but no full proofs appear in this text, and the models are 'available at [27]' with no URL given. The comparison with Finkbeiner et al. is mostly qualitative, plus one note that their method times out on an 8-bit leakage bound.

rq2.prover_cost: NA

rq3.speedup_and_baseline: ZK Hats verified in 6.34s; no speedup over a baseline reported

rq4.statement_proven: Soundness of the ZK Hats interactive protocol: a cheating prover succeeds with probability at most 2^-R
rq4.proof_system_used: Simple interactive challenge-response ZK puzzle
rq4.reason_for_choice: Used as the motivating example of a soundness quantitative hyperproperty

cq.note: Uses machine-checked verification of protocol soundness; the paper does not study any ZK failure class.

rq5.limitations: Verification conditions, invariants, trace enumeration relations and Skolem witness functions all have to be written by hand, and each needs application-specific insight. The method handles only QHPs with a single quantifier alternation.
rq5.open_problems: Automating verification-condition generation and inferring quantified invariants.

eligibility.note: NIZK arguments of knowledge are a core mechanism for publicly verifying the notary set and signature validity in DeTAPS.

eligibility.note: The paper machine-checks the security of the zero-knowledge proofs of shuffle by Terelius-Wikström and Bayer-Groth, so ZKPs are its primary subject.

qa.evidence: Completeness, l-special soundness and HVZK are proven in Coq, with a failure event (commitment binding broken). A dedicated limitations section covers side channels, Fiat-Shamir, code extraction and efficiency. Verification took 16m13s on a single core of an Intel i5 MacBook Pro, against 7m40s for the Swiss Post implementation.

rq2.proof_size: Bayer-Groth proof size is sublinear in the number of ciphertexts (asymptotic)
rq2.prover_cost: NR
rq2.verifier_cost: Bayer-Groth verification time is roughly a third of Terelius-Wikström's

rq3.workload: Shuffle of 6,400 votes, each encrypted in two ElGamal ciphertexts (25,600 ciphertexts including input and output), in a 2048-bit safe-prime group
rq3.speedup_and_baseline: Extracted OCaml verifier: 16 min 13 s; Swiss Post Java implementation: 7 min 40 s on the same machine (roughly half the speed)

rq4.statement_proven: The output ciphertexts are a re-encrypted permutation of the input ciphertexts (relation Rpk)
rq4.proof_system_used: Bayer-Groth 9-round proof of shuffle and Terelius-Wikström 5-round proof of shuffle (sigma-like protocols)
rq4.reason_for_choice: These are the most prominent proofs of shuffle in practice; Bayer-Groth is used by Swiss Post and Scytl

cq.note: Found that the Terelius-Wikström proposition claims completeness and HVZK for Rpk∨Rcom, which does not hold; a refined claim was machine-checked. Fiat-Shamir is discussed only as future work.

rq5.limitations: Only the interactive variants are machine-checked, not the Fiat-Shamir transform, and Coq extraction is unverified. Side channels are not covered, and the extracted verifier runs at about half the speed of the Swiss Post implementation.
rq5.open_problems: Machine-checked reasoning about the Fiat-Shamir transform and rewinding of random oracles, and checking strong Fiat-Shamir in the Swiss Post implementation. Verified optimisations of the verifier.

eligibility.note: The paper presents a front-end compiler (Buffet) that turns C programs into constraints for the zkSNARK back-end Pinocchio/GGPR, and it supports the zero-knowledge property.

qa.evidence: The paper defines End-to-end Completeness and Soundness and relies on the cited GGPR/Pinocchio proof of knowledge and on collision resistance for soundness. It gives constraint-cost formulas and measured setup and prover times on a 16-core Xeon E5-2680 with 32 GB RAM, compared against BCTV and Pantry. It says the source code is public (ref [1]) and has a section on limitations.

rq2.proof_size: 288 bytes (libsnark Pinocchio, 128-bit security)
rq2.prover_cost: |C|·60 µs + |C| log|C|·0.9 µs
rq2.verifier_cost: 6 ms + (|x|+|y|)·3 µs per instance; setup |C|·180 µs

rq3.workload: 9 benchmarks (matrix multiplication, PAM clustering, Fannkuch, pointer chasing, merge sort, Boyer-Moore, KMP search, RLE decoding, sparse matrix-vector multiplication), each up to about 10M constraints
rq3.speedup_and_baseline: Matches Pantry on straight-line code, which is 2-4 orders of magnitude better than BCTV; 1-2 orders better than BCTV and 2-3 orders better than Pantry on RAM; 1-2 (up to 3) orders better than BCTV/BuffetStatic on data-dependent control flow
rq3.memory: Runs are limited by testbed RAM (32 GB) to about 10M constraints

rq4.statement_proven: y = Psi(x) for C programs that use RAM and data-dependent control flow
rq4.proof_system_used: Pinocchio (GGPR) via libsnark
rq4.reason_for_choice: Used as a common back-end so that front-ends can be compared; it is modular and optimized

cq.note: NR

rq5.limitations: Constraints are not universal, so setup amortizes worse than BCTV, and there is no support for function pointers or goto. Prover overhead and setup costs are still too high for general practical use.
rq5.open_problems: What is the right combination of programming language and execution model for compiling to constraints? Can higher-level language features be supported without a machine abstraction?

eligibility.note: The paper presents Geppetto, a QAP/Pinocchio-based commit-and-prove scheme (MultiQAPs) with perfect zero-knowledge, bounded proof bootstrapping and a compiler for verifiable computation.

qa.evidence: Formal definitions are given, with Theorems 1-6 proving binding, knowledge soundness and perfect ZK under q-PKE, q-PDH and q-SDH (some lemma proofs are omitted and cited to PGHR). The available text has only headline claims (up to two orders of magnitude, five orders over bootstrapped systems, MNT estimated 34-77x slower); the evaluation section (§7) is cut off. The code is only planned for release ('plan to make the code available').

rq2.proof_size: Constant-size proof per sub-QAP plus one commitment per bus; constant-size proof and commitment with bounded bootstrapping
rq2.prover_cost: Linear/quasilinear in circuit size; MultiQAP raises the degree by only 1 per shared state element (vs. tens or hundreds with Merkle trees); energy-saving circuits cost only the path actually taken
rq2.verifier_cost: Linear in the number of commitments and proofs; constant after bootstrapping

rq3.workload: C programs compiled through LLVM (clang) by an F# compiler with a C++ crypto runtime; MapReduce, loops, cryptographic computations, bootstrapping
rq3.speedup_and_baseline: Up to two orders of magnitude lower cost for sharing state (vs. Merkle-hash approaches); five orders of magnitude over prior bootstrapped systems (Ben-Sasson et al.); MNT-cycle approach estimated 34-77x slower than Pinocchio-style proofs (11x slower for the pairing part)

rq4.statement_proven: Correct execution of outsourced C computations with shared state (MapReduce, loops), crypto operations on signed data, and secret proprietary algorithms
rq4.proof_system_used: Geppetto (Pinocchio-derived MultiQAP CP scheme on a BN curve, plus a Cocks-Pinch curve for bounded bootstrapping)
rq4.reason_for_choice: Reduce prover overhead and add flexibility over Pinocchio; native embedding of crypto operations; the MNT cycle is too costly at 128-bit security

cq.note: NR

rq5.limitations: Bounded bootstrapping requires committing in advance to the maximum number of proofs, which costs some universality; verifier costs grow linearly without bootstrapping.
rq5.open_problems: Finding efficient pairing-friendly curve cycles at 128-bit security; automated QAP partitioning (only partially explored with METIS).

eligibility.note: Presents a program-to-circuit compiler framework for (zk-)SNARKs with new circuit-friendly algorithms (arithmetization-level).

qa.evidence: Gives constraint counts compared with Buffet, Geppetto, Cinderella and manual ZeroCash implementations. Formal SNARK security definitions are omitted and deferred to existing papers. Says it plans to open source the framework in the near future, but gives no URL.

rq2.proof_size: NR
rq2.prover_cost: Read-only memory: k(2√n + log2 n) constraints for k accesses; long-integer multiplication: 2m−1 constraints (O(m))

rq3.workload: SHA-256, SWIFFT, RSA-2048 modular exponentiation, AES-128, sorting, ZeroCash Pour circuit
rq3.speedup_and_baseline: SHA-256: 26155 constraints vs 44999 (Buffet) and 38556 (Geppetto); RSA-2048: 90804 vs 144933 (Cinderella/Geppetto), >1.5x; AES-128 (300): 4.2×10^6 vs 9.3×10^6† (Buffet) and 27.2×10^6† (Geppetto); read-only memory 3-10x vs optimized alternatives (n=256); ZeroCash: 3.8×10^6 vs 4×10^6 (manual)

rq4.statement_proven: Correct execution of user programs compiled to circuits (e.g., hashes, RSA, AES, ZeroCash Pour)
rq4.proof_system_used: libsnark preprocessing zk-SNARK (QAP)
rq4.reason_for_choice: Emits a libsnark-compatible format; the back-end SNARK is not the contribution

cq.note: Uses overflow tracking for bitwidth safety but does not study circuit failures.

rq5.limitations: Optimal bitwidth adjustment through nonlinear optimization does not scale to large circuits, and the greedy strategies are not always optimal. Multivariate polynomial minimization can take exponential time, so constraints are clustered into bounded-size groups.
rq5.open_problems: Extending the techniques to recursive SNARK composition is mentioned but not developed. The evaluation counts constraints only.

eligibility.note: Defines and constructs zero-knowledge SNARKs over authenticated data (AD-SNARK), a QAP-based ZK proof system.

qa.evidence: Formal definitions plus proofs of completeness, adaptive PoK under q-PKE/q-DHE and statistical ZK. Concrete benchmarks vs AD-PGHR (e.g., prover 491 s vs 20 s) are reported. Evaluation section is only partially included, so hardware details are not visible.

rq2.proof_size: Secret-key verification: constant (0.4 KB); public verification: linear in the number of authenticated inputs (126 KB for 50K gates and 1000 authenticated inputs; under 170 KB for a monthly bill)
rq2.prover_cost: Same as PGHR plus 3 multi-exponentiations with N terms; 20 s for 50K gates and 1000 authenticated inputs (vs 491 s for AD-PGHR)
rq2.verifier_cost: Secret-key: 0.035 s; public: 0.61 s (linear in N: signature checks plus a multi-pairing)

rq3.workload: Arithmetic circuit with 50K multiplication gates and 1000 authenticated inputs; smart-metering billing
rq3.speedup_and_baseline: Up to 24.5x prover speedup, 18.7x key generation speedup and 19.9x smaller proving key vs AD-PGHR (generic libsnark/BSCTV14 with in-circuit signatures) at 128-bit security

rq4.statement_proven: Satisfiability of an arithmetic circuit on inputs authenticated by a trusted source, without revealing the inputs (e.g., a correct bill computed from signed meter readings)
rq4.proof_system_used: ADSNARK, an extension of PGHR/Pinocchio (BSCTV14) with an embedded linearly homomorphic MAC
rq4.reason_for_choice: Encoding signature verification inside a QAP costs more than 1000 multiplication gates per signature; the embedded MAC avoids this cost

cq.note: NR

rq5.limitations: Public verification loses constant-size proofs, and its proof size and verification time grow linearly with the number of authenticated inputs. Security relies on the non-falsifiable q-PKE assumption.
rq5.open_problems: Extensions to multiple data sources and (amortized) constant-time verification are covered in the appendix.

eligibility.note: The paper designs hardware for the prover and verifier of a GKR/CMT sumcheck-based interactive proof for verifiable computation, which is a succinct-argument building block, although the paper says the system has no zero-knowledge property.

qa.evidence: Soundness error ε=(⌈log|y|⌉+5d log G)/|F| is unconditional and follows from the cited GKR analysis. A cost model is validated against synthesis and cycle-accurate RTL simulation (area error +7.6% to +11%). Limitations are discussed in §9, e.g. the high price of verifiability and the absence of ZK and public verifiability.

rq2.proof_size: NR (communication per auxiliary input is d·(log G+2)+1 field elements; 2b sumcheck rounds per layer)

rq2.verifier_cost: O(d·log G+|x|+|y|) online, plus offline precomputation of O(d·G) per auxiliary input

rq3.workload: Layered arithmetic circuits (d=20, G=2^14, δ=0.5); NTT with 2^6 to 2^13 points over Fp, p=2^63+2^19+1; Curve25519 point multiplication
rq3.speedup_and_baseline: Compared with a native trusted-node ASIC baseline (prover at 7 nm untrusted, verifier at 350 nm trusted): for 2^10-point NTT Zebra is competitive, on larger NTTs better by 2–3×; with several hundred elliptic-curve point multiplications in parallel, about 2×
rq3.memory: Verifier storage d·(log G+2)+1 field elements per auxiliary input; prover buffer is dG·nP,pl
rq3.energy: Field op energy: 45 nm add 0.006 nJ, mul 0.21 nJ; 350 nm add 3.1 nJ, mul 220 nJ; total power 121–140 W for NTT designs (Pmax=150 W)

cq.note: The paper targets hardware Trojans via verifiable computation, not proof-system failures.

rq5.limitations: Zebra beats the baseline only with more than a decade's technology gap and large arithmetic-friendly computations, and it costs orders of magnitude more than untrusted execution. It requires trusted precomputation delivered on storage and lacks ZK, public verifiability and low round complexity.
rq5.open_problems: Comparing costs across foundries and technology nodes is described as a research question; broadening applicability beyond computations naturally expressed as arithmetic circuits.

eligibility.note: The paper improves the T13/CMT/GKR sum-check interactive proof for succinct verifiable outsourcing; the proof is not zero-knowledge, but sum-check/GKR is a succinct-argument building block.

qa.evidence: Soundness holds unconditionally with error (⌈log|y|⌉+6d log(G·N))/|F|, and Appendix A gives the proofs. Prover cost drops from O(d·N·G·log G) to O(d·(N·G+G·log G)), and the evaluation uses cycle-accurate simulation with stated technology nodes, Amax and Pmax against native and Zebra baselines. Source code is at http://www.pepper-project.org/, and Section 9 discusses limitations.

rq4.proof_system_used: T13 (CMT/GKR variant) with the Giraffe refinements
rq4.reason_for_choice: Suits hardware, fits the data-parallel model so precomputation amortizes, and has low overhead compared with the alternatives

rq5.open_problems: Combine with vSQL-style polynomial commitments to handle non-deterministic ACs. Confirm that control-logic costs are negligible and extend the program transformations.

eligibility.note: Anonymous payment channels whose core mechanism is NIZK proofs of knowledge over commitments, blind signatures and range proofs.

qa.evidence: The paper gives formal anonymity and balance games, and Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 point to proofs in the full version. The prototype reports Pay timings on a Xeon E5-2695 v4 over 1000 iterations and compares them with Tumblebit's 387ms. Abort and anonymity limitations are discussed in detail.

rq2.prover_cost: Bidirectional Pay customer 100.13 ± 1.60 ms (CL-Sigs), 37.61 ± 0.93 ms (algebraic MACs)

rq3.speedup_and_baseline: Tumblebit at 387ms per channel payment is 5 times slower than the Bolt bidirectional prototype

rq4.proof_system_used: Camenisch-Stadler style ZK proofs of knowledge with CL signatures or algebraic MACs and Pedersen commitments

eligibility.note: Proposes a new sum-check/GKR-style interactive proof for verifiable CNN convolution, which is a succinct-argument building block, although the protocol itself has no zero-knowledge property.

eligibility.note: Implements and optimizes the GKR interactive proof and sum-check-based streaming interactive proofs for verifiable computation, which are succinct-argument building blocks, though the protocols do not use zero-knowledge.

qa.evidence: Theorems 3.2-3.4 and 4.1 give the prover and verifier costs, with proofs in Appendix A and citations to [19] and Schwartz-Zippel. The experiments ran in C++ on AMD Opteron machines with 32 GB of RAM over the field with p=2^61-1, and the paper reports concrete times and compares against baselines (NI, MRS, the bounded protocol). The source code is cited as [16], but the extracted text gives no URL.

rq2.prover_cost: O(S(n) log S(n)) for GKR (vs poly(S(n))); O(n log n) for NI F2 via FFT; O(n log^2 n) for linearization
rq2.verifier_cost: Space O(log S(n)); time O(n log n + d(n) poly(log S(n)))

eligibility.note: New sigma-protocol ZK proofs (batched range proofs, CS/ElGamal consistency, shuffle) are the core mechanism for achieving malicious security in PSI-sum.

qa.evidence: Ideal/real security model with q-DHI and Strong RSA assumptions; proofs in appendices. Table 3/4/6 give communication, computation and monetary costs vs DDH-based semi-honest, HEK12, RR17b. Hardware only partly stated (Intel Xeon E5, 3.75 GB); no code URL.

rq2.proof_size: Batched sigma protocols ~ cost of a single sigma protocol; Bayer-Groth shuffle/multi-exponentiation proofs O(sqrt(n)); malicious-security overhead can be sublinear O(sqrt(n)) communication
rq2.prover_cost: O(n log n) computation in the sublinear-communication regime; linear in n otherwise (Table 2 operation counts)

rq3.workload: Shuffled DOPRF / PSI-sum on sets of size 2^12, 2^16, 2^20; 1536-bit safe RSA moduli, NIST prime256v1
rq3.speedup_and_baseline: Communication 4.21-5.03x over semi-honest DDH protocol (low-comm setting); 25x monetary cost of semi-honest; 250x less communication and 65x lower monetary cost than HEK12 generic MPC at 2^20; ~1.5x cost of RR17b DE-ROM one-sided PSI

rq4.statement_proven: Correct DOPRF evaluation, CS/ElGamal encryption consistency with range proofs, correct shuffle and re-randomization, correct partial decryption, correct parameter generation
rq4.proof_system_used: Sigma protocols (Fiat-Shamir), Bayer-Groth shuffle and multi-exponentiation arguments, Camenisch-Shoup verifiable encryption
rq4.reason_for_choice: Sigma protocols allow efficient proofs over committed/encrypted values and batching to reduce communication; avoid generic ZK and trusted setup

cq.note: Verifiable parameter generation is used to avoid trusted setup, not as a study of setup failures.

rq5.limitations: Computation costs are much higher than semi-honest and SCS approaches (e.g., 284,075 s at 2^20 in low-comm setting). Intersection sum must lie in a polynomial domain so that exponential ElGamal can be decrypted.
rq5.open_problems: NR

eligibility.note: IntegriDB is an authenticated data structure for verifiable SQL that uses bilinear accumulators and Merkle/skip-list trees; it has no zero-knowledge property, and ZK SNARKs (libsnark, SNARKs for C) appear only as related work and baselines.

qa.evidence: Security is defined by an ADS experiment and rests on q-SBDH and an extractability assumption, with proofs only sketched. Evaluation on EC2 with 16GB RAM uses TPC-H/TPC-C and synthetic tables and compares against libsnark and SNARKs for C. Code is linked at integridb.github.io, and Section 5.2 lists limitations.

rq2.proof_size: O(d log n) for d-dim range; Õ(|R|) for JOIN; 27.97KB JOIN on 100,000-row tables; 84,296 Bytes sum on 10-dim range (1,000 rows)
rq2.prover_cost: Setup O(sum m_i^2 n_i); 168s JOIN on 100,000 rows; ~5000s 10-dim range on 100,000 rows
rq2.verifier_cost: O(d log n + |R|); 45.4ms JOIN; ~400ms 10-dim range on 100,000 rows

rq3.workload: TPC-H query #19 (lineitem 6M rows), TPC-C, synthetic tables up to 100,000 rows
rq3.speedup_and_baseline: Setup and prover time 10x faster than libsnark and 100x faster than SNARKs for C (estimated), on a sum over a 10-dim range query with 1,000 rows; verification 10x slower and proofs 200x larger
rq3.memory: Server storage 1.85GB for 10^5 rows x 10 columns (table itself 30MB)

rq4.statement_proven: Correctness of SQL query results (JOIN, multidimensional range, SUM/COUNT/AVG/MAX/MIN, limited nesting) over an outsourced database
rq4.proof_system_used: Bilinear accumulator ADS for set operations with sum, plus authenticated interval trees (skip list)
rq4.reason_for_choice: Generic circuit/RAM VC is inefficient for database-sized programs and does not support efficient updates

cq.note: NR

rq5.limitations: Short proofs are not supported for comparisons between columns, aggregations among columns, or a JOIN with duplicates inside a nested query. Storage is quadratic in the number of columns and setup is costly.
rq5.open_problems: Supporting LIKE queries in a dynamic database; removing the no-duplicates assumption for a JOIN on a range result.

eligibility.note: PEREA is an anonymous authentication scheme in which users run ZKPoK protocols to prove that their recent tickets are not in an accumulator and that a signed queue is intact; ZKPs are the core mechanism.

qa.evidence: Formal security games are defined, and the security theorem rests on Strong RSA and DDH; Appendix B gives only a proof sketch. The prototype ran on a 2.0 GHz Core2 laptop and was compared with BLAC: server time was 0.05s (K=5) and 0.16s (K=30), versus 2.9s for BLAC at L=800. The discussion covers timing attacks, the lack of concurrent security, the choice of K and unblacklisting cost.

rq2.proof_size: O(K) communication between user and SP (uplink); downlink O(L) blacklist with 166-bit entries
rq2.prover_cost: O(L) + O(K·ΔL) at the user; e.g. 0.7s for K=10 with ΔL=100, worst case 5.9s for L=800
rq2.verifier_cost: O(K) at the server; 0.05s for K=5 and 0.16s for K=30

rq3.workload: PEREA authentication with K=5,10,15,30 and blacklist sizes up to 800; C with OpenSSL 0.9.8g on a Lenovo T60 (2.0 GHz Core2 T7200, 1.5 GB RAM), single-threaded
rq3.speedup_and_baseline: Server time 0.05s (K=5) and 0.16s (K=30), versus 2.9s for BLAC at L=800; blacklist download 16.24 KB versus 113.67 KB for BLAC (L=800); user-side time is slower than BLAC

rq4.statement_proven: Knowledge of a CL-signed queue whose last K tickets are non-members of the blacklist accumulator, plus a well-formed current ticket and a commitment to the next queue
rq4.proof_system_used: Sigma-style ZKPoK (Camenisch–Stadler notation) over a Strong RSA group, combining a universal accumulator (Li et al.) and CL signatures
rq4.reason_for_choice: Lets the SP revoke users without a TTP, with server cost independent of blacklist size

cq.note: Timing-attack linkage is countered by adding a delay; the scheme is not concurrently secure, so authentication runs must be sequential.

rq5.limitations: The ZKPoK is not secure under concurrent execution, so the SP has a critical section that can limit throughput, and user-side computation is higher than in BLAC. Unblacklisting forces O(L) witness updates, and a small K limits how often users can authenticate when misbehavior takes a long time to detect.
rq5.open_problems: Remove the sequential critical section.

eligibility.note: The paper builds succinct non-interactive arguments: it boosts the succinctness of batch arguments (BARGs) and gives SNARGs for deterministic time-T and RAM computation, a core succinct-argument topic.

qa.evidence: Theorems 1.3 and 1.4 state the contribution, and formal definitions and proofs are given (Theorems 5.2 and 6.3). Asymptotic proof sizes poly(λ,m,log k) and poly(λ,log T) are compared with CJJ21a/b, HJKS22 and WW22. There is no implementation; caveats are given only in passing, such as quasi-polynomial security under the subexponential variant.

rq2.prover_cost: NR
rq2.verifier_cost: L(k,λ)·poly(s) for index BARG; L(T,λ)·poly(S,ℓ) for flexible RAM SNARG

rq4.statement_proven: Batch NP (BatchCSAT) statements; RAM computation M(x)=y with respect to a digest
rq4.proof_system_used: Generic boosting of any non-trivial seBARG via flexible RAM SNARGs with partial-input soundness and fully local SEH
rq4.reason_for_choice: Reach polylogarithmic succinctness from weakly succinct BARGs under falsifiable standard assumptions

cq.note: NA

rq5.limitations: Starting from a BARG with only (log k)^ω(1) succinctness requires subexponential assumptions, and the resulting security holds only against quasi-polynomial-time adversaries. The results apply to publicly verifiable, read-only RAM computation and need rate-1 string OT.
rq5.open_problems: Build any non-trivial BARG (one that beats sending all witnesses) from new assumptions; the paper's result then turns it into fully succinct BARGs and SNARGs for P.

eligibility.note: Proposes a pairing-based accumulator with a zero-knowledge proof of knowledge of an accumulated value, used for revoking anonymous credentials; the ZK proofs are a core mechanism.
